kingdoms.name: Cinderfall Compact
kingdoms.text: Once a furnace kingdom, now a city of elected ward stewards beneath a surviving royal works charter. Its cheap heat depends on clay cylinders whose owners were never allowed to withdraw their voices. Repair guilds want public control; charter houses insist the furnaces are their inheritance. A bent copper reed is the old sign that a household will shelter a stranger.

kingdoms.name: Veyran Glass March
kingdoms.text: Mountain towns joined by suspended freight lines, governed by competing mooring councils. Their engineers sold the Crown a sky network in return for winter fuel. Families measure kinship by who will hold the other end of a safety rope. Veyr served its engineering tradition; his personal failure does not represent every Marcher.

kingdoms.name: Serein River Covenant
kingdoms.text: Floodplain settlements share water through seasonal assemblies rather than a permanent king. Cinderfall acquired their sluices through emergency debt after a disastrous flood. River witnesses keep parallel oral and written surveys because either can be altered. Riven's signature made a political decision look like an unavoidable natural event.

kingdoms.name: Thornwake Orchard Holds
kingdoms.text: Independent orchard communities descend from displaced furnace workers and older woodland settlements. Land passes with duties to graft, share water and leave paths open. Some growers accept Crown ash fertilizer; others fear the voices it carries. Corin's living cutting is ordinary cultivation made politically dangerous by the claim that only machines can preserve a future.

kingdoms.name: Aster Bellward
kingdoms.text: A former pilgrim kingdom survives as scattered rain chapels, observatories and refuge houses. Bellkeepers disagree about whether sacred recordings may ever be repeated. Hesper belongs to the answering tradition: a bell must leave time for another bell. Its royal line is gone; the sacred authority claimed by the Crown is a later appropriation.

towns.name: Cinderfall
towns.text: Built around shared furnace heat, its lanes follow buried steam pipes. The festival began as a day when the works stopped and every household sang in its own time. Employers turned it into a synchronized production anthem. Mara still leaves one chair empty without claiming the person will return.
towns.ambient: A repair stitch crosses every festival banner; no family can afford a whole new one.

towns.name: Lowbank
towns.text: Raised walkways link rooms marked with successive flood heights. Residents were promised drainage when they surrendered their river rights. Wiremother exploits a real tradition of adults singing children home through fog. Its borrowed lullaby is theft, not proof that mothers became monsters.
towns.ambient: Two door handles sit at different heights: one for dry weather, one for flood boats.

towns.name: Brakehaven
towns.text: The rail refuge grew from a brakekeepers' siding where workers hid passengers from winter requisitions. Brass once enforced the same orders the refuge resisted. Its inn charges for a bed but never for sitting beside the stove.
towns.ambient: Every bunk has a red cord reaching the emergency brake.

towns.name: Siltcross
towns.text: A ferry town divided by the flood plan Riven signed. Survey stones survive below the mud, contradicting the official accident report. Rebuilding a living bank and opening a ferry are both useful commitments with different timescales.
towns.ambient: The ferryman leaves the erased flood year on his tariff board.

towns.name: Rainbell
towns.text: A chapel settlement whose missing quarter was erased from both maps and tax rolls. Families still set bowls on absent doorsteps during the first rain. Hesper remembers names without demanding that everyone repeat the same account.
towns.ambient: Rain collects on a doorstep with no house behind it.

towns.name: Ledger Quay
towns.text: Porters carry cylinders into archive warehouses while clerks bill repeated voices as fresh labor. Mira's numbered record is part of a system that makes people transferable assets. The quay also houses clerks who secretly preserve corrections.
towns.ambient: A ledger has a column for wages and none for permission.

towns.name: Glassreach
towns.text: Its suspended docks prospered by lifting freight above toll roads. The mooring councils accepted military contracts to keep winter supplies moving. Veyr's daughter belonged to a household here; the repeating glass voice cannot replace her.
towns.ambient: A safety rope is knotted into a wedding loop beside the dock.

towns.name: Ember Orchard
towns.text: A settlement rebuilt around trees that survived a furnace fire. People graft damaged trunks rather than hide the scars. The Cinder Seed is a runaway cultivation mechanism, not a judgment on those who needed its harvest.
towns.ambient: New fruit grows above an old burn scar.

towns.name: Unfinished Row
towns.text: Work houses were sold by installment to the people who built the furnaces. Rook's father helped build machinery that harmed neighbors and left a house neither completed nor paid for. His apology can be read; it cannot repair the house by itself.
towns.ambient: An unopened room still has its builder's chalk marks.

towns.name: Passwatch
towns.text: A border station became a settlement because refugees waited there for papers that never arrived. Couriers learned to deliver orders without seeing those affected. Sable's uniform once made him safe at the expense of people outside the gate.
towns.ambient: The outgoing road is wider than the waiting shelter.

towns.name: Lensward
towns.text: An observatory town supported by lens grinders, shepherds and signal keepers. Its star charts were intended to warn travelers, then repurposed to predict and police movement. Reopening crossings gives the instruments a public use again.
towns.ambient: A star chart has weather stains along its safest walking route.

towns.name: Warmstep
towns.text: A winter settlement of kitchens, clinics and rope stores. Heat tariffs make survival a debt. Residents disagree over which public room should open first, while still feeding each other's children. Their need exists before the heroes arrive.
towns.ambient: Soup bowls warm on a rail once reserved for freight.

peoples.name: Furnace households
peoples.text: Households include blood relatives, apprentices and lodgers sharing heat bills. Some support the charter because they fear losing winter fuel; others organize the work stoppage. They speak in practical promises, not mechanical slogans.

peoples.name: Riverfolk
peoples.text: An overlapping set of boat families, farmers and survey keepers, not a separate biological species. Different settlements dispute flood responsibility. Their expertise comes from work and teaching, not mystical blood.

peoples.name: Bellkeepers
peoples.text: An order open to newcomers, split between preservation and answering traditions. Some helped erase dangerous testimony to protect their chapels. Others sheltered its witnesses.

peoples.name: Numbered survivors
peoples.text: People classified as archive subjects or industrial assets. They have different origins and ambitions; Mira does not speak for all of them. A number imposed by an institution is never their natural identity.

peoples.name: Glass Marchers
peoples.text: Riggers, council families, refugees and lens workers share the mountain routes. Wealth and contractual power divide them more than ancestry. Safety customs coexist with exploitative freight debts.

peoples.name: Graftkeepers
peoples.text: Orchard workers who inherit responsibilities alongside growing rights. Newcomers may join by tending a common tree. Their arguments concern labor and land as much as sacred memory.

peoples.name: Charter retainers
peoples.text: Soldiers, couriers and clerks paid by the Crown's institutions. Some knowingly profit, some obey, some defect. Brass and Sable must answer for choices rather than a supposedly evil ancestry.

peoples.name: Clay-bound echoes
peoples.text: Recorded phrases may sound responsive without being a living person. The campaign provides no proof that a recorded fragment contains the whole speaker. Never treat destroying equipment as killing the original person, or manufacture consent from a repeated yes.

weapons.name: Courier's edge
weapons.text: A road blade sized to cut harness and clear wreckage. The works issued heavier guards to trusted couriers; the stamp records service, not innocence. Its eventual meaning is keeping a passage open rather than carrying another sealed order.

weapons.name: Regulator hammer
weapons.text: A workshop tool whose tuned head seats copper reeds without cracking their clay sockets. His father's mark remains beneath the grip. Repairing with it acknowledges an inheritance without excusing what that inheritance built.

weapons.name: Clinic staff
weapons.text: A walking support wound with washable cloth, carried between households when the clinic runs out of beds. The ferrule taps a recognizable arrival rhythm so patients need not fear a patrol.

weapons.name: Brake iron
weapons.text: A rail lever retained after his last official order. Notches mark inspections rather than victories. Used in defense, it turns an instrument of confinement toward stopping a train.

weapons.name: Survey hook
weapons.text: A boat hook with measured rings for reading water depth. The official flood mark was filed away; the rings underneath survive. Its reach is practical river equipment before it is a weapon.

weapons.name: Index needles
weapons.text: Thin archive tools used to lift cylinder labels without damaging them. Mira refuses the clerk's habit of discarding a damaged label. Their precision belongs to restoring identities, never to treating people as specimens.

weapons.name: Mooring lance
weapons.text: A sectional conductor pole used to catch and ground sky cables. The insulating grip was repaired at home. Its reach cannot bridge the distance between a repeated voice and a living child.

myths.name: The First Potter
myths.text: Children hear that a potter saved winter songs in clay. The missing verse says she returned each vessel to the singer when spring came. The charter kept the first half and suppressed the return.
myths.truth: The pottery floor dates show separate recordings. Sable's mother gave a particular gift; no myth turns it into permanent permission.

myths.name: The Crown Beneath the Furnace
myths.text: Workers say a buried king keeps the heat alive. Royal propaganda treats this as proof that the city requires one ruler.
myths.truth: HollowCrown is a directing mouth of the network. Breaking it ends a local regime while leaving its distributed machinery running.

myths.name: The River That Keeps Names
myths.text: Boat families say the river remembers everyone it takes. This offers mourners a way to speak, not a promise of recoverable voices.
myths.truth: The uncensored survey, not a supernatural river verdict, reveals who ordered the flood.

myths.name: The Answering Bell
myths.text: A pilgrim leaves a gap after ringing so a distant house can reply. Later authorities call silence a flaw to be corrected.
myths.truth: Different registers can cooperate without becoming identical. The mountain relay turns that teaching into an actionable sequence.

myths.name: The Child Behind Glass
myths.text: Sky workers tell children a window can hold a last farewell. The tale became a sales pitch for endless preservation.
myths.truth: A recorded child cannot hear a present answer; the living child outside still can.

myths.name: The Song Without an Ending
myths.text: Growers sing a verse and let the next worker change it. Charter editions print a final authoritative refrain.
myths.truth: The Choir fears forgetting so much that it forbids revision. Its defeat leaves people responsible for what they remember together.

myths.name: Rook’s Wayglass and the Resonance Paths
myths.text: Mineral Mako holds repeatable patterns: heat, weight, motion or the steadying rhythm a healer can shape. A core supplies the pattern; a support changes its shape; a person learns to carry it through the Resonance Paths. Rook’s folding Wayglass locates rare seams by finding a clear route through every reflection. It records no voices and contains no captive person. A found crystal must be recovered, attuned on the Paths, and fitted to a linked socket before it changes a technique.

plot.name: A stolen household song
plot.text: The theft of Nell's father's voice gives Sable an immediate rescue. The familiar recording creates a question, not a resurrection promise.

plot.name: The carriage manifest
plot.text: Prison transport connects the festival theft to an organized supply chain. Brass can help but cannot call his past orders harmless.

plot.name: Water carries evidence
plot.text: Riven knows the river routes the cylinders use. His evasions make the route useful and his silence costly.

plot.name: An erased neighborhood
plot.text: A missing quarter proves the archive can remove people from public memory without removing their surviving neighbors.

plot.name: Labor after death
plot.text: The ledgers charge repeated words as continued work. The theft is an economic system, not a single collector's obsession.

plot.name: The network above town
plot.text: The sky engine shows how widely the machinery reaches. Veyr's skill comes with responsibility for the design.

plot.name: Something living survives
plot.text: Corin's cutting offers continuity through change. The crew can carry a future without freezing a past.

plot.name: The false ending
plot.text: HollowCrown falls. Keep its local victory real while the still-running pumps and relays foreshadow unfinished work.

plot.name: The voice that lures
plot.text: Wiremother uses copied affection to draw children in. Rescue takes priority over Sable's hope of hearing his mother again.

plot.name: Orders have authors
plot.text: Brass admits signing the prison order. The surviving flood evidence connects administrative violence to the river.

plot.name: The flood was chosen
plot.text: Riven owns his signature. Public repair begins with acknowledging who paid for the old plan.

plot.name: Names beyond Mira
plot.text: Mira restores other people's names without a guaranteed answer about herself. Publication and safety remain distinct concerns.

plot.name: An apology cannot build
plot.text: Rook reads the letter he avoided. Grief and culpability coexist; neither cancels the other.

plot.name: The child who can answer
plot.text: Veyr confronts a loop that cannot hear him while a living child needs help. Do not stage that child as a replacement daughter.

plot.name: The courier chooses
plot.text: Sable admits obedience had consequences and opens a refugee route. Taking off the uniform becomes an action.

plot.name: Many registers
plot.text: The relays cooperate without forced unison. The network begins to expose the scale of its demand for a single answer.

plot.name: The sky becomes useful
plot.text: Lens repair reveals crossings and warnings. Previous victories remain worthwhile even when they did not finish the struggle.

plot.name: People need warmth now
plot.text: The crew commits scarce resources to a clinic or kitchen. The city is not suspended until its final boss dies.

plot.name: Wings for passengers
plot.text: A freight route carries people. Veyr's responsibility is to travelers rather than machinery's abstract success.

plot.name: The inconvenient witness
plot.text: The unedited account implicates the crew's side as well. A good cause does not license a cleaner invented history.

plot.name: The gift had limits
plot.text: Recording dates prove separate sessions. The mother's freely given voice is not consent to indefinite extraction.

plot.name: The Choir breathes
plot.text: The intake and miners reveal preservation's material cost. Turning the vent outward rescues workers before the final argument.

plot.name: A city without one owner
plot.text: The assembly starts a school or archive before the confrontation. No vacant throne waits for Sable to inherit.

plot.name: Leave room for an answer
plot.text: The Choir offers perfect retention at the price of every future voice. Sable still wants his mother, but refuses to make that desire law. The final gap breaks imposed unison. Preserve the existing private or public recording choice and return the reed case to Mara.

monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Bramble Wolf
monsters.text: Pack hunters carry hooked burrs between woodland patches. Broken migration corridors put them against travelers on narrow roads. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Inkfold Crane
monsters.text: It nests in waste-paper reeds and stains its feathers with archive dyes. Clerks call it an omen because it gathers where discarded records accumulate. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Shellstream Otter
monsters.text: Shell tools crack river mussels. Flood gates destroyed the shallow feeding banks, so adults defend the remaining wells. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Basalt Salamander
monsters.text: It basks on warm mineral seams. Reactor waste has concentrated its food near machinery that workers must approach. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Candlebranch Stag
monsters.text: Waxy secretions protect new antler growth. Orchard lantern makers gather shed flakes; living animals should not be harvested. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Copper Quill
monsters.text: Mineral-coated quills discharge built-up static. Railworkers first mistook the flashes for broken electrical contacts. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Stormsilk Manta
monsters.text: It rides rising warm air along mountain faces. Sky moorings and storm anchors occupy the same wind lanes. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Elder Rootstone Golem
monsters.text: Roots have grown through abandoned jointed stoneworks. Its movements defend water and growing space rather than a forgotten king's commands. Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.
monsters.elder: Older specimens have survived more disturbed seasons. Elder is an age and encounter variant, not a separate people or a new origin myth.

monsters.name: Kiln Teapot Mimic
monsters.text: A discarded communal kettle learned the pressure rhythm of the works. Habitat: Old kitchens and Lowbank. Boiling-over salute: leave the marked circle before it lands. Its pressure behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Reedwheel Serpent
monsters.text: Its crest turns in a current; broken gates drive it into drinking channels. Habitat: River wells and spillways. Sluice-ribbon rush: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its siphon behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Clockwork Mole
monsters.text: A burrowing maintenance creature plates its shell with discarded rail metal. Habitat: Rail embankments. Survey-claw trench: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its forge behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Folio Heron
monsters.text: It gathers waterlogged pages for nesting, preserving scraps clerks tried to discard. Habitat: Archive marshes. Margin-cut dive: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its erase behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Blossomback Boar
monsters.text: Bark armor protects living grafts carried between surviving trees. Habitat: Burned orchards. Graft-root charge: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its pressure behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Sootveil Lynx
monsters.text: It hunts by the breaks in machinery noise and steals focus with its ash veil. Habitat: Reactor vents. Smokestack feint: leave the marked circle before it lands. Its siphon behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Brasswing Dragonfly
monsters.text: Grounding wires imitate the reed stems where it lays its eggs. Habitat: Sky cables. Copper-thread dart: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its tempo behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Frostgill Axolotl
monsters.text: Its crystalline gills regrow after the polluted water sheds their outer scales. Habitat: Cold cisterns. Coldwater fan: leave the marked circle before it lands. Its molt behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Cracked Kiln Knight
monsters.text: An obsolete heat tender still tries to shield the furnace that once housed it. Habitat: Abandoned rail kilns. Hearth-door sweep: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its forge behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Vesper Bell Orchid
monsters.text: Its flowers answer nearby tones, leaving a pause between each bloom. Habitat: Rain chapels. Petal-bell hush: leave the marked circle before it lands. Its chorus behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Glasshorn Ram
monsters.text: Glass mineral seams grow into its horns; dropped climbing rope tangles in its fleece. Habitat: Mountain workshops. Prism-horn charge: step sideways from the marked line before it lands. Its tempo behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.

monsters.name: Memory-ring Nautilus
monsters.text: Its shell records seasons as growth rings, without recording anyone’s voice. Habitat: Flooded foundations. Undertow refrain: leave the marked circle before it lands. Its siphon behavior changes how it responds in battle.
monsters.elder: An original species of the living and industrial landscape.
